title: Binary Tree Paths
statement: `root` is the root of a non-empty binary tree. A leaf is a node that has neither a left nor a right child. For every leaf, take the path that starts at `root` and goes down to that leaf, and write it as a string: the node values from top to bottom, in decimal (with a leading `-` for negative values), separated by the two characters `->`. Return the list of these strings, one per leaf, in any order.
constraints: The tree has between 1 and 100 nodes
notes:
## Intuition

Each answer string is just the sequence of values met while walking from the root down to one leaf. A depth-first walk naturally follows such a path: as it descends it can carry the text built so far, and when it lands on a node with no children, that text is a finished answer. Strings are immutable, so each call simply builds a longer copy for its children and nothing has to be undone on the way back up.

## Approach

1. Keep a list `paths` and call `dfs(root, '')`.
2. In `dfs(node, path)`, extend the text: `current` is the value alone for the root, otherwise `path + '->' + node.val`.
3. If `node` has no left and no right child, it is a leaf: push `current` into `paths` and stop.
4. Otherwise recurse into each child that exists, passing `current` along.
5. After the walk, return `paths`.

## Example 1, step by step

The tree `[1,2,3,null,5]` has root 1 with children 2 and 3, and 5 as the right child of 2. `dfs(1, '')` makes `current = "1"`. It goes left to `dfs(2, "1")`, giving `"1->2"`; node 2 has only a right child, so it calls `dfs(5, "1->2")`, which makes `"1->2->5"` and, being a leaf, stores it. Back at the root, `dfs(3, "1")` builds `"1->3"`, another leaf. The result is `["1->2->5", "1->3"]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · h): every node is visited once, and building each `current` copies up to h values, where h is the height.
- Space: O(n · h) in the worst case for the output strings, plus O(h) for the recursion.

## Pitfalls

- A node with exactly one child is not a leaf; only push when both children are missing, or a path like `"1->2"` sneaks in.
- Do not put `->` before the first value or after the last one.
- Negative values already print their own `-`, giving text like `"0->-1"`; do not add or strip signs.
- Equal values on different branches can produce equal strings; keep both.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `paths` | finished root-to-leaf strings |
| `node` | the node `dfs` is visiting |
| `path` | text of the path from the root down to `node`'s parent |
| `current` | `path` extended with `node`'s value |

narration.2: Collect every finished root-to-leaf string here.
narration.4: Visit node, knowing the text of the path above it.
narration.5: Append this node's value, with an arrow unless it is the root.
narration.6: No left and no right child means this node is a leaf.
narration.7: The path is complete, so record it.
narration.8: A leaf has nothing below it; go back up.
narration.10: If there is a left child...
narration.11: ...continue the path down the left side.
narration.13: If there is a right child...
narration.14: ...continue the path down the right side.
narration.18: Start the walk at the root with an empty path.
narration.19: Every leaf has been reached; return all the paths.
